patent: Filed 2010-02-11 by Fanuc Ltd (priority JP 2009-030876, 2009-02-13), issued 2012-02-07, one claim. A parallel robot of delta configuration (the text says delta-type only for the prior art of FIG. 11): three arms translate a platform without turning it, and three long rods driven from motors on the fixed base turn a three-axis wrist hung under the platform, for six degrees of freedom in all. The prior art in FIG. 11 has one rotation axis at the platform, driven through a single telescopic arm. FIGS. 1-4 show the design of an earlier application (the text does not identify it), and FIG. 1 is the front-page drawing, so the drawing printed on the front page is not the claimed wrist. The new element starts at FIG. 5: the tool face is cut at an angle to the sixth axis, so the common tool-straight-down pose no longer coincides with the wrist singularity. The singular pose still exists, at a tilted tool attitude. Claim 1 combines that inclined face with the holder-assembly drive and the nested gear train. The delta configuration is generally credited to Reymond Clavel at EPFL in the 1980s (US 4,976,582).

figs.9B: The same assembly cut 90 degrees around 44a from FIG. 9A, so 48a now lies in the page and 46a is the oblique one. figs.10: Rod 54 at a working tilt: 54a leans away from the vertical 44a, and inner holder 48 with member 78 leans with it inside holder 46, while 44 stays vertical. Motor 52 turns 44 through output shaft 76 and gear 74 (no teeth drawn). The motor body hangs below its mounting plate and shaft 76 ends level with the gear, leaving the space above 44 clear for the rod to swing.
figs.11: Prior art, shown for contrast. Numerals 205a to 207b appear on one arm only; the other two arms repeat it. glossary.def: A manipulator whose platform is carried by several linked chains side by side rather than by one serial arm, which keeps moving mass low and stiffness high.
A parallel robot with three arms rotated at the shoulder, each ending in a pair of parallel rods. The parallelograms keep the platform from turning, so it only translates.
The patent's term for one arm: a driving link (upper arm) plus a parallel pair of driven links (forearm).

A pose where a robot loses a direction of motion and its joint solution is not unique. Here axes 4 and 6 are parallel: rotation about them can be shared between the two in any split, and no axis supplies rotation about the remaining direction (gimbal lock). Six-axis arms have the same wrist singularity when axis 5 is at zero.

Two crossed pivots that pass rotation between shafts at an angle; also Cardan joint. One joint alone gives a non-uniform output speed at an angle, but two in series with parallel end shafts and phased yokes give equal input and output speed, which fits the patent's statement that the holder 44 and the input shaft 101 turn at the same angular velocity.
Nested rings pivoted on perpendicular axes. The patent does not use the word, but holders 44, 46 and 48 form one, with the rod sliding through the innermost ring.
A hinge: a joint allowing one rotation between two bodies.
A linear guide whose nut runs on recirculating balls in grooves along a shaft, so the shaft slides freely but cannot turn in the nut and can carry torque.
The tool at the end of a robot, such as a gripper; the patent's hand 122.

Japanese patent publication types: kokai is the unexamined laid-open publication, kokoku the examined one. Column 1 prints Examined Patent Publication (kokai) for JP4-45310B; the examined type and the B suffix point to kokoku.
